findings.source_passage: left it like the complicated ribbed bed of a torrent, when the rushing waters have been dried up
findings.source_locator: paragraph 1, description of the stranger's pox-scarred face
findings.why_it_matters: The full simile is stylistically distinctive and characteristic of Melville's descriptive voice; the draft reduces it to 'ribbed his face like a torrent's bed,' losing the evocative 'rushing waters have been dried up' completion that gives the image its desolation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full simile: 'like the complicated ribbed bed of a torrent, when the rushing waters have been dried up.'

findings.source_passage: I know many chaps that hav'n't got any,—good luck to 'em; and they are all the better off for it. A soul's a sort of a fifth wheel to a wagon.
findings.why_it_matters: The setup—'I know many chaps that hav'n't got any, good luck to 'em; and they are all the better off for it'—is essential context that makes the fifth-wheel line land with its full sardonic punch; the draft delivers the punchline without the build, flattening Elijah's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full speech: 'I know many chaps that hav'n't got any,—good luck to 'em; and they are all the better off for it. A soul's a sort of a fifth wheel to a wagon.'

findings.source_passage: He's got enough, though, to make up for all deficiencies of that sort in other chaps, abruptly said the stranger, placing a nervous emphasis upon the word he.
findings.why_it_matters: This moment—the sudden, emphasis-laden reference to Ahab's superabundant soul—is interpretively important: it introduces the theme of Ahab's metaphysical excess and establishes Elijah's prophetic register. Its absence removes a key beat of the encounter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Elijah's italicized interjection about 'He's got enough, though,' with the narratorial note about the nervous emphasis on 'he.'

findings.source_passage: both commenting, after each other's fashion, upon this ragged old sailor; and agreed that he was nothing but a humbug, trying to be a bugbear
findings.source_locator: final paragraphs, after Elijah names himself
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'after each other's fashion' is a characteristic Ishmaelian aside that gently signals the comedy of Ishmael-Queequeg miscommunication; the draft replaces it with 'counting him a humbug bugbear,' losing the ironic qualification.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'both commenting, after each other's fashion' to preserve the narrator's wry awareness of the cross-cultural pair.

findings.source_passage: It is the easiest thing in the world for a man to look as if he had a great secret in him.
findings.source_locator: near end, Ishmael's challenge to Elijah
findings.why_it_matters: This line is gently ironic and self-undermining—Ishmael's bravado immediately before being unsettled—and carries tonal weight as a voice marker for the narrator's defensive rationalism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the line as Ishmael's parting retort before Elijah gives his name.

summary: No high-severity signature losses; the draft preserves the chapter's key lines and the closing catalogue of Ishmael's anxieties faithfully, but several medium- and low-severity flattenings trim Elijah's full sardonic voice and cut a small but interpretively charged beat about Ahab's soul.
